---
title: "Why does earning more feel like it should have fixed things by now?"
pubDate: "2026-08-17"
description: "You hit the salary you used to dream about. The anxiety did not leave with the old pay stub."
---

You had a number in your head. Maybe it was £40k, maybe £60k, maybe more. You told yourself — not out loud, just quietly, in the background — that once you got there, the tight feeling in your chest before you checked your account would stop.

It did not stop.

This is one of the more disorienting things Joel hears from clients. They are earning well. Objectively, the numbers work. And yet the relationship with money feels exactly as fraught as it did when the numbers were smaller. Sometimes worse, because now there is no obvious excuse.

The behaviour underneath tends to be one of a small number of patterns. Some people avoid looking altogether — the account balance sits unchecked for weeks because checking feels like an accusation. Some people earn and spend in a loop that keeps the balance roughly where it was three years ago, regardless of the income. Some people check constantly, track every transaction, and still feel as though catastrophe is one unexpected bill away.

None of these are character flaws. They are learned responses to earlier experiences with money — responses that made sense at the time and are now running in the background of every financial decision.

The first thing Joel usually asks a new client is not "what are your goals?" It is closer to: what does your money actually do when you are not paying attention to it? The answer tends to be more revealing than any spreadsheet.

If you want to find out which pattern fits your current relationship with money, the quiz below takes about four minutes.
